He was shot in Chihuahua on 26 June 1811, together with Allende, Jiménez and Santa María, and his head was displayed in Guanajuato.

personas/mariano-matamoros/resumen.texto: Born in Mexico City and priest of Jantetelco, he was denounced for sympathizing with the insurgency, escaped and joined Morelos at Izúcar on 16 December 1811. Morelos made him a colonel and lieutenant general, his second in command: according to one source during the siege of Cuautla (February to May 1812), and according to another after Morelos's entry into Oaxaca (May 1813). After the failure before Valladolid (23–24 December 1813) he was defeated by Iturbide at Puruarán (5 January 1814), during the retreat, captured and shot on 3 February. Morelos proposed exchanging him for Spanish prisoners, but the proposal was not accepted.

personas/francisco-morazan/resumen.texto: Honduran liberal who distinguished himself at the battle of La Trinidad (November 11, 1827). In April 1829 he overthrew the government of Mariano Beltranena and Mariano Aycinena, took Guatemala, and captured Arce together with them, and he governed de facto until the Congress elected José Francisco Barrundia interim president on June 25. He was president of the Federal Republic of Central America from 1830 to 1839, as well as head of state of Honduras and El Salvador. His liberal reforms (freedom of the press, civil marriage, separation of Church and State) provoked a war with the conservatives. In 1829 he ordered the expulsion of Archbishop Ramón Casáus and of friars from several orders, and his government and that of Mariano Gálvez confiscated Church property and abolished the tithe. In 1840 his attempt to restore the federation by arms, the invasion of Guatemala, failed before Carrera. In 1842 he arrived in Costa Rica, obtained the departure of Braulio Carrillo through the Pact of Jocote, and made himself head of state; an uprising against his war plans overthrew him, and he was executed by firing squad in San José on September 15.

personas/rafael-carrera/resumen.texto: Mestizo peasant from Guatemala City, illiterate, who in 1837 led the rural revolt against the liberal government of Mariano Gálvez, with the support of the clergy and amid a cholera epidemic. With Indigenous and mestizo peasants from the east and south he took Guatemala on 13 April 1839, defeated Morazán in March 1840 and subdued Los Altos: in April 1840 he had most of the liberal officials of the Quetzaltenango town council shot. With this the federation was broken. He dominated Guatemala as military chief from 1839 and was president in 1844–1848 and again from 1851, for life from 1854, until his death in 1865. The liberals, who returned to power in 1871, discredited him, while other authors, such as Ralph Lee Woodward Jr. in his 1993 biography, stress his support for the Indigenous peasantry.

personas/manuel-jose-de-arce/nombre.texto: Manuel José de Arce y Fagoaga

personas/manuel-jose-de-arce/resumen.texto: Salvadoran, first president of the Federal Republic of Central America (1825–1829). José Cecilio del Valle received more votes from the electors (41 to 34), but Congress, which had a liberal majority, ruled that he did not have an absolute majority and elected Arce with conservative votes. Arce lost liberal support and, from 1826, Congress stopped meeting. He ousted the liberal governor of Guatemala, Juan Barrundia, and the rebellion in El Salvador started a civil war. He left the presidency on 24 February 1828 in the hands of Vice President Mariano Beltranena, who refused to hand it back. In April 1829 Morazán overthrew Beltranena and arrested Arce.

personas/dionisio-de-herrera/resumen.texto: Honduran liberal lawyer, uncle and guardian of Francisco Morazán. He was head of state of Honduras (1824–1827) and of Nicaragua (1830–1833), when both were states of the Federal Republic of Central America.

personas/juan-mora-fernandez/resumen.texto: Costa Rican teacher and politician, the first head of state of Costa Rica (1824–1833), within the Federal Republic. His policy of distributing land favored the rise of coffee, and during his government the country's first printing press arrived.

personas/braulio-carrillo/resumen.texto: Costa Rican lawyer, head of state of Costa Rica in 1835–1837 and dictator from 1838 to 1842. On 14 November 1838 he declared Costa Rica a sovereign and independent state, separate from the Federal Republic. He reorganized the administration, codified the laws, punished vagrancy and expanded the powers of the executive. Morazán invaded Costa Rica in 1842, and Carrillo, in exile, was murdered in El Salvador in 1845.

personas/juan-lindo/resumen.texto: Honduran lawyer who was the last alcalde mayor of the province of Comayagua in 1821, promoter of the annexation of Central America to the Empire of Iturbide and, in 1838, from the Honduran constituent assembly, of his country's separation from the Federal Republic. He was head of state of El Salvador (1841–1842) and president of Honduras (1847–1852).

personas/francisco-ferrera/resumen.texto: Honduran military officer who served Morazán at La Trinidad and Gualcho, and in October 1838 rebelled against the federal government so that Honduras would be a free state. Morazán defeated him in April 1839, but he continued the war against Morazán and supplied Carrera with arms. President of Honduras from 1841 to 1844 (in 1833–1834 he had been provisional head of state).

personas/juan-galindo/resumen.texto: Irishman born as John Galindo in Dublin, naturalized as a Central American in 1829, an official of Morazán's liberal government, military governor of Petén, and sent to Washington and London over the Belize dispute. In 1831 he travelled the Usumacinta River and explored Palenque, and in 1834 Copán, whose reports he illustrated. He is considered a pioneer of Maya archaeology: he was one of the first to copy the glyphs carefully and treat them as writing, and he proposed that the cities had been built by the ancestors of today's Maya. He died on 30 January 1840 at the end of a battle near Tegucigalpa, in the civil war, fighting with the liberal army.

personas/mateo-aleman/resumen.texto: Sevillian novelist, author of the picaresque novel Guzmán de Alfarache (1599 and 1604). In 1608 he went to New Spain and arrived in Mexico City in the retinue of Archbishop García Guerra, whose favor he enjoyed. There he published the Ortografía castellana (1609), which defended writing as one pronounces, and the Sucesos de don fray García Guerra (1613). According to recent research (Cartaya Baños, 2011) he died in Mexico City in 1614; an earlier source had him alive in 1615.

personas/juan-ruiz-de-alarcon/resumen.texto: Novohispanic playwright of the Spanish Golden Age, born in Taxco around 1581 (he himself said he was from Mexico City). He studied canon law at the Royal and Pontifical University of Mexico and law at Salamanca. He returned to New Spain around 1607–1608, earned a licentiate in law from the University of Mexico in 1609, and unsuccessfully sought a professorship. In 1611 he went to Spain with Viceroy Luis de Velasco, Marquis of Salinas; there he wrote La verdad sospechosa and from 1625 served on the Council of the Indies. He died in Madrid in 1639.

personas/melchor-muzquiz/resumen.texto: Student at the Colegio de San Ildefonso who left it to join the insurgency (in 1810 or early 1811, according to the author). He fought in Michoacán and Veracruz under Ignacio López Rayón and Guadalupe Victoria, rose to colonel and was captured at the Monte Blanco hacienda. A pardon saved him from being shot, although he refused to swear that he would not take up arms against Spain again. In 1821 he joined the Plan of Iguala. He was later governor of the State of Mexico (1824) and interim president of Mexico in 1832.

personas/antonio-lopez-de-santa-anna/res.texto: Military officer from Xalapa who joined the Veracruz Fixed Regiment in 1810, at the age of 16, under Colonel José Joaquín de Arredondo, and fought the insurgents as a royalist officer, including in Texas (Battle of Medina, 1813). In 1821 he switched to the Plan of Iguala. In December 1822 he proclaimed, with Guadalupe Victoria, the Plan of Veracruz against Iturbide, and the Plan of Casa Mata (February 1823) precipitated the fall of the First Mexican Empire, which ended with Iturbide's abdication on 19 March. His later role in independent Mexico was central: president on several occasions between 1833 and 1855, the loss of Texas and the war with the United States.

personas/lucas-alaman/resumen.texto: Naturalist, businessman and politician from Guanajuato. In 1810 he witnessed the sacking of the Alhóndiga de Granaditas by Hidalgo's troops, an event that shaped his conservative thinking. In 1820–1821 he was a deputy for New Spain in the Spanish Cortes in Madrid, while the Plan of Iguala advanced. His Historia de Méjico (five volumes, 1849–1852) is the main conservative history of the war of 1808–1821 and a counterweight to the insurgent sources. He later served as minister of foreign relations and was a figure of the Conservative Party; he died in 1853.

personas/francisco-de-ceinos/resumen.texto: Jurist from Toro, prosecutor of the Council of the Indies, and judge of the second Audiencia of Mexico from 1530; he returned to New Spain in 1560. He presided over the Audiencia, which governed between the death of Viceroy Luis de Velasco (1564) and the arrival of the Marquis of Falces (1566), and again between July and November 1568. In 1565 he wrote to Philip II a memorial on settlement policy that denounced the Indigenous mortality since the conquest; he died in Mexico City between 1568 and 1569.

personas/gaston-de-peralta/nombre.texto: Gastón de Peralta, Marquis of Falces

personas/gaston-de-peralta/resumen.texto: Navarrese born in Pau, third viceroy of New Spain (1566-1568). He arrived while the conspiracy of Martín Cortés, Marquis of the Valley, was being tried: he suspended the execution of Luis Cortés and was accused by the Audiencia judges of protecting the conspirators. Philip II sent visitors who had him return to Spain, where he underwent a residencia and was acquitted. His ordinance of 1567 protected an area around Indigenous lands, a precursor of the fundo legal.

personas/luis-carrillo/resumen.texto: Doctor and court official, appointed by Philip II in 1567 as commissioner together with the licentiates Gaspar de Jarava, who died on the voyage, and Alonso Muñoz, to investigate the government of the Marquis of Falces after the Cortés conspiracy. They arrived at Veracruz on October 29, 1567, ordered the viceroy's return to Spain, and tried the accused with torture, sentences to the galleys, confiscations, and banishments; the Crown later recalled them because of the colonists' complaints. He died in 1568 on the voyage from Veracruz to Havana. Some lists of governors count him among the viceroys, but he was a visitor: the government passed to Muñoz and then to the Audiencia.

personas/lorenzo-suarez-de-mendoza/nombr.texto: Lorenzo Suárez de Mendoza, Count of La Coruña

personas/lorenzo-suarez-de-mendoza/resum.texto: Fifth Count of La Coruña and fifth viceroy of New Spain (October 4, 1580, to June 29, 1583), successor to Martín Enríquez, who went to Peru. To curb corruption in the Audiencia he asked the king for a visitor, who was Pedro Moya de Contreras, and, according to the lists of governors, he created the Consulado, which was founded in 1592. He died in the capital, still in office.

personas/luis-de-villanueva-y-zapata/res.texto: Doctor from Salamanca and senior judge of the Audiencia of Mexico. When the Count of La Coruña died in June 1583, he governed New Spain on an interim basis until September 24, 1584, when Pedro Moya de Contreras, already influential as visitor, took office.

personas/alvaro-manrique-de-zuniga/nombr.texto: Álvaro Manrique de Zúñiga, Marquis of Villamanrique

personas/alvaro-manrique-de-zuniga/resum.texto: Son of the Dukes of Béjar and first Marquis of Villamanrique, viceroy of New Spain from 1585 until January 1590. He formed militias to defend the Pacific ports after the raids of the corsair Thomas Cavendish (1587), and he eased the Chichimec War through negotiation and the handing out of supplies. Because of his clash with the Audiencia of Guadalajara and with the regular clergy, Bishop Diego Romano, a visitor, tried him and attached his property. The royal decree (cédula) of 1599 that rehabilitated him and his will of 1601-1602 show him alive in Seville, where he died on March 3, 1604; some lists of governors give him as dead around 1590.

personas/pedro-de-otalora/resumen.texto: Guipuzcoan, judge of the Audiencia of Mexico from 1597 and priest from 1609. As president of the Audiencia he governed New Spain between the death of Viceroy García Guerra (February 22, 1612) and the arrival of Diego Fernández de Córdoba (October 18). On May 2, 1612, he presided over the tribunal that sentenced 35 Black people to death for rebellion; afterward he was president of the Audiencia of Guadalajara.

personas/diego-carrillo-de-mendoza/nombr.texto: Diego Carrillo de Mendoza, Marquis of Gelves

personas/diego-carrillo-de-mendoza/resum.texto: Military man from Valladolid, viceroy of Aragon and, from September 21, 1621, viceroy of New Spain. He fought banditry, distributed grain during the famine of 1623, and confronted the merchants who monopolized maize. His conflict with Archbishop Juan Pérez de la Serna ended in the riot of January 15, 1624: the palace was partly burned and he had to flee; the Crown replaced him with the Marquis of Cerralvo. Sources give his death between 1631 and 1636.

personas/lope-diez-de-aux-y-armendariz/n.texto: Lope Díez de Aux y Armendáriz, Marquis of Cadreita

personas/lope-diez-de-aux-y-armendariz/r.texto: Naval officer born around 1575 in Quito or in Charcas, according to the source, son of the president of those audiencias, and the first Creole to govern New Spain (September 1635 to August 1640). He founded the Armada de Barlovento, based in Veracruz, and continued the drainage of the Valley of Mexico, with the Nochistongo canal after the earthquake of 1637. He was succeeded in August 1640 by the Duke of Escalona, with whom Juan de Palafox came as a visitor to judge his government. He died in Madrid; some works say only that he was alive in 1640.

personas/diego-lopez-pacheco/nombre.texto: Diego López Pacheco, Duke of Escalona

personas/diego-lopez-pacheco/resumen.texto: Duke of Escalona and Marquis of Villena, viceroy of New Spain from August 28, 1640 to June 10, 1642; he arrived with Juan de Palafox, commissioned to try his predecessors. He strengthened the Armada de Barlovento and authorized a Jesuit expedition to California. After the 1640 revolt of Portugal, his kinship with the Duke of Braganza, proclaimed king, made him suspected of disloyalty, and Palafox replaced him. Palafox had him arrested and confiscated his property; in Spain he was declared innocent, refused to return to office, and was later viceroy of Navarre.

personas/marcos-de-torres-y-rueda/resume.texto: Bishop of Yucatan from 1646, he governed New Spain from May 13, 1648 to April 22, 1649, with the title of governor and president of the Audiencia, not of viceroy, although the lists count him among the viceroys; he died in the capital; some sources place his birth around 1588. The outgoing viceroy resisted handing over the office, and the intervention of the Crown was needed. In April 1649 the auto de fe of the Volador was held, with 13 executed and 94 or 99 flogged, depending on the source.

personas/matias-de-peralta/resumen.texto: Jurist born in Arequipa, oidor of Quito and from 1636 of the Audiencia of Mexico. As senior oidor he presided over the Audiencia that governed New Spain from the death of Viceroy Torres y Rueda (April 22, 1649) until the arrival of the Count of Alba de Liste (June 1650). The visitor Pedro de Gálvez suspended him in November 1650 and again in 1651; he died in relative poverty in 1655.

personas/francisco-fernandez-de-la-cueva.texto: Francisco Fernández de la Cueva, 8th Duke of Alburquerque

Born in Barcelona, soldier in Flanders (Rocroi, 1643) and general of the cavalry of Catalonia, viceroy of New Spain from August 15, 1653 to September 15, 1660, and afterward of Sicily. Facing war with England, he reinforced Veracruz and San Juan de Ulúa and sent arms to Jamaica, Cuba and Florida. He pushed ahead with the works of the cathedral of Mexico and in 1659 had the buildings that encroached on its atrium torn down.

personas/juan-francisco-de-leyva-y-de-la.texto: Juan Francisco de Leyva y de la Cerda, Count of Baños

Mariner from Alcalá de Henares, Marquis of Adrada and Count of Baños, viceroy of New Spain from September 16, 1660 to June 28, 1664. His government is remembered for the abuses of his family, the complaints of the nobility and the town councils, and a rebellion in Tehuantepec in 1661, in which the bishop of Oaxaca mediated. The Crown removed him for corruption, forbade him to serve at court, and he ended his days as a Carmelite friar.

personas/diego-osorio-de-escobar/nombre.texto: Diego Osorio de Escobar y Llamas

personas/diego-osorio-de-escobar/resumen.texto: Galician, inquisitor and vicar in Toledo, bishop of Puebla from 1656 until his death; he refused the archbishopric of Mexico in 1663. He was interim viceroy of New Spain from June 29 to October 15, 1664, in place of Leyva y de la Cerda, and resigned as soon as he could to return to his diocese. In those months he reformed the postal service and founded a gunpowder factory.

personas/antonio-sebastian-de-toledo/nom.texto: Antonio Sebastián de Toledo, Marquis of Mancera

personas/antonio-sebastian-de-toledo/res.texto: Son of the viceroy of Peru, he fortified Corral and Valdivia in 1645 and was ambassador in Venice and Germany. Viceroy of New Spain from October 15, 1664 to December 8, 1673, he reorganized the Armada de Barlovento and completed the interior of the cathedral of Mexico, which was dedicated a second time in 1667. He and his wife were patrons of Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz. The works give his birth as 1621 or 1622.

personas/tomas-de-la-cerda-y-aragon/nomb.texto: Tomás de la Cerda y Aragón, Marquis of La Laguna

personas/tomas-de-la-cerda-y-aragon/resu.texto: Marquis of La Laguna and consort count of Paredes, viceroy of New Spain from 1680 to 1686. On his entry, triumphal arches were erected by Carlos de Sigüenza y Góngora and by Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, whose patron he was. He took office on November 30, 1680, months after the revolt of the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico (August 10), which had broken out under Friar Payo Enríquez de Rivera.

personas/juan-de-ortega-y-montanes/resum.texto: Inquisitor, bishop of Durango, Guatemala and Michoacán, and from 1700 archbishop of Mexico; his birthplace is placed in Llanes, Siles or Cartagena, depending on the source. He was interim viceroy of New Spain twice: from February 27 to December 1696, when he put down the students' riot at the university and supported the Jesuit expedition to California, and from November 4, 1701 to November 1702.

personas/francisco-fernandez-de-la-cueva.texto: Francisco Fernández de la Cueva, 10th Duke of Alburquerque

Genoese by birth, captain general of the coast of Granada and of Andalusia, viceroy of New Spain from November 27, 1702 to November 13, 1710, in the midst of the War of the Spanish Succession. He was a supporter of Philip V, fought banditry with summary executions on the roads, and under his government the town of Alburquerque, in New Mexico, which bears his title, was founded in 1706. He received the Order of the Golden Fleece for his services in New Spain; he died in Madrid.

personas/baltasar-de-zuniga-duque-de-ari.texto: Baltasar de Zúñiga, Marquis of Valero and Duke of Arión

Second son of the Duke of Béjar, viceroy of Navarre and of Sardinia, and viceroy of New Spain from August 16, 1716 to October 14, 1722. He ordered the expulsion of the British from Laguna de Términos (1716) and survived a knife attack in 1718. In 1719 he created the Tribunal de la Acordada, a summary court against banditry, and during his government San Antonio de Béjar was founded (1718). He later became president of the Council of the Indies.

personas/juan-de-acuna-marques-de-casa-f.texto: Juan de Acuña y Bejarano, Marquis of Casa Fuerte

Born in Lima, he was the second Creole to govern New Spain, from October 15, 1722 until his death on March 17, 1734. He raised the revenue of the treasury, authorized the resumption of the Gaceta de México in 1728, rebuilt the Mint and built the customs house. In 1731 the families from the Canary Islands who founded the town of San Fernando arrived at the presidio of San Antonio de Béjar.

personas/pedro-de-castro-duque-de-la-con.texto: Pedro de Castro Figueroa y Salazar, Duke of La Conquista

Galician military man, president of the kingdom of Sicily (1735–1737) and viceroy of New Spain from August 17, 1740 until his death on August 22, 1741. A British frigate stopped his ship near Puerto Rico and he lost his credentials. During the war with Great Britain under Edward Vernon, he reinforced the garrison of St. Augustine in Florida and the defense of the Caribbean of New Spain.

personas/pedro-malo-de-villavicencio/res.texto: Native of Seville, he arrived in New Spain in 1709 and was prosecutor and a member of the Audiencia of Mexico. As president of the Audiencia he governed the viceroyalty from the death of the Duke of La Conquista (August 22, 1741) until the arrival of the Count of Fuenclara in 1742; sources give April or November 1742.

personas/juan-francisco-de-guemes-conde-.texto: Juan Francisco de Güemes y Horcasitas, Count of Revillagigedo

Captain general of Cuba (1734–1746) and first Count of Revillagigedo, viceroy of New Spain from July 9, 1746 to November 9, 1755. He promoted the colonization of New Santander, under José de Escandón, and the pacification of Sonora after the Pima revolt. He was the father of Juan Vicente de Güemes, viceroy from 1789 to 1794.

personas/agustin-de-ahumada-marques-de-l.texto: Agustín de Ahumada y Villalón, Marquis of Las Amarillas

Military man born in Ronda and governor of Barcelona, viceroy of New Spain from November 10, 1755 until his death on February 5, 1760. During his government, in 1756, the patronage of the Virgin of Guadalupe over New Spain, which Benedict XIV had confirmed in 1754, was celebrated, and work on the drainage of the capital continued.

personas/francisco-antonio-de-echavarri/.texto: Native of Vitoria, knight of the Order of Santiago and oidor, president of the Audiencia of Mexico. He governed on an interim basis between the death of Viceroy Ahumada (February 5, 1760) and the arrival of Cajigal (April 28). Earlier, from 1739, he had been visitor of the mines of Zacatecas, where he clashed with the great mine owners, and he took charge of the aqueduct of the Villa de Guadalupe.

personas/francisco-cajigal-de-la-vega/re.texto: Lieutenant general from Cantabria and governor of Cuba from 1747 to 1760. When Ahumada died, the sealed dispatches of the Audiencia named him interim viceroy of New Spain: he entered the capital on April 28, 1760 and governed until October, when the Marquis of Cruillas took office. He reduced taxes on iron and steel products and raised the regular army to 2,921 men.

personas/joaquin-de-montserrat-marques-d.texto: Joaquín de Montserrat, Marquis of Cruillas

Native of Valencia, viceroy of New Spain from October 6, 1760 to August 24, 1766. He organized a colonial army with militias and faced the smallpox epidemic of 1761, the Maya rebellion of Jacinto Canek (1761) and the revolt of the Pimas and Seris in Sonora.

personas/carlos-francisco-de-croix/nombr.texto: Carlos Francisco de Croix, Marquis of Croix

personas/carlos-francisco-de-croix/resum.texto: Military man born in Lille, captain general of Galicia and viceroy of New Spain from August 25, 1766 to September 22, 1771. With the visitor José de Gálvez he carried out the expulsion of the Jesuits on June 25, 1767. The revolts that the expulsion provoked in Guanajuato, Pátzcuaro, Valladolid and Uruapan were put down by hanging their leaders, and his proclamation warned that subjects “were born to keep silent and obey.” The works give his birth between 1699 and 1703 and his death between 1778 and 1786.

personas/antonio-maria-de-bucareli/nombr.texto: Antonio María de Bucareli y Ursúa

personas/antonio-maria-de-bucareli/resum.texto: Native of Seville, lieutenant general and governor of Cuba (1766–1771), viceroy of New Spain from 1771 until his death on April 9, 1779. He reorganized the treasury and coinage, fortified Acapulco and Perote, promoted the settlement of Alta California and sent a naval expedition to Alaska.

personas/martin-de-mayorga/resumen.texto: Field marshal from Barcelona, captain general of Guatemala from 1773 to 1779, during the Santa Marta earthquake. When Bucareli died, the sealed instructions of the Crown designated the captain general of Guatemala: he governed New Spain from August 23, 1779 to April 28, 1783 and reinforced Havana and Veracruz in the war against Great Britain.

personas/francisco-roma-y-rosell/resumen.texto: Catalan jurist, born in Mataró or in Figueras (around 1710 or in 1727, depending on the source), and first regent of the Audiencia of Mexico. He governed on an interim basis between the death of Bucareli (April 9, 1779) and the arrival of Mayorga (August 23). He wrote about the guilds of Barcelona (1766) and in 1768 Signs of the Happiness of Spain, which defended the development of agriculture, industry and trade.

personas/matias-de-galvez-y-gallardo/res.texto: Native of Málaga, from Macharaviaya, brother of José de Gálvez and father of Bernardo de Gálvez. Captain general of Guatemala (1779–1783), where he recovered the fortress of San Fernando de Omoa, he was viceroy of New Spain from April 29, 1783 until his death on November 3, 1784.

personas/vicente-de-herrera-y-rivero/res.texto: Jurist from Santander, student at the Colegio de San Bartolomé in Salamanca, criminal judge (alcalde del crimen) and oidor of the Audiencia of Mexico and regent of that of Guatemala. He was interim viceroy of New Spain from October 20, 1784, when Matías de Gálvez, ill, delegated command, until June 17, 1785, when Bernardo de Gálvez took office. First Marquis of Herrera (1790).

personas/eusebio-sanchez-pareja/resumen.texto: Governor of New Galicia and president of the Audiencia of Guadalajara (1771–1776 and 1777–1786). With Bernardo de Gálvez already very ill, the Audiencia named him interim viceroy on November 9, 1786; he continued until May 8, 1787, when Alonso Núñez de Haro took office. In 1780 he had a map of New Galicia drawn up.

personas/manuel-antonio-florez/resumen.texto: Mariner from Seville, viceroy of New Granada (1776–1781) and of New Spain (August 17, 1787 to October 16, 1789), and afterward captain general of the Royal Navy. He resigned in New Granada in November 1781, after the Comuneros rebellion.

personas/miguel-de-la-grua-talamanca/nom.texto: Miguel de la Grúa Talamanca, Marquis of Branciforte

personas/miguel-de-la-grua-talamanca/res.texto: Sicilian, brother-in-law of the royal favorite Manuel de Godoy, viceroy of New Spain from July 12, 1794 to May 31, 1798. He appropriated part of the property confiscated from French (1794) and British (1797) residents of New Spain and sold offices and military ranks; the Mexico City council accused him of squandering public funds, and his biographers count him among the most corrupt viceroys.

personas/miguel-jose-de-azanza/nombre.texto: Miguel José de Azanza, Duke of Santa Fe

personas/miguel-jose-de-azanza/resumen.texto: Navarrese, secretary of the visitor José de Gálvez, minister of War with Godoy (in 1793 or in 1795–1796, depending on the source) and viceroy of New Spain from May 31, 1798 to April 30, 1800; in November 1799 he had those involved in the Machete Conspiracy arrested, which had been denounced before they could act. He later collaborated with Joseph Bonaparte and died in Bordeaux.

personas/felix-berenguer-de-marquina/res.texto: Mariner from Alicante, professor of mathematics and astronomy at the Academy of Cartagena, governor and captain general of the Philippines until 1793 (from 1787 or 1788, depending on the source) and viceroy of New Spain from April 30, 1800 to January 4, 1803.

personas/pedro-de-garibay/resumen.texto: Field marshal from Alcalá de Henares, in New Spain since 1764. After Gabriel de Yermo's coup against Iturrigaray (September 15, 1808), the Audiencia named him viceroy: he governed from September 16, 1808 to July 19, 1809 and was succeeded by Archbishop Lizana. That same night the Creole autonomists of the town council were imprisoned: Francisco Primo de Verdad died in the archbishop's prison and Friar Melchor de Talamantes in San Juan de Ulúa.

personas/pedro-catani/resumen.texto: Jurist from Barcelona, oidor of the Audiencia of Santa Fe during the Comuneros rebellion (he signed the 1782 sentence against its leaders), interim governor of Santo Domingo in 1788, and regent of the audiencias of Guadalajara (1804) and of Mexico (1807). In September 1808 he was, with the oidores Aguirre and Bataller, among the promoters of the coup against Viceroy Iturrigaray, and he asked for the arrest of Friar Melchor de Talamantes. As regent he presided over the Audiencia that governed New Spain between the departure of Archbishop Lizana (May 8, 1810) and the arrival of Venegas (September 14); he died around 1815.

personas/francisco-javier-venegas/nombre.texto: Francisco Javier Venegas, Marquis of La Reunión de Nueva España

personas/francisco-javier-venegas/resume.texto: Military man born in Zafra, defeated at Uclés (1809) and military governor of Cádiz in 1810. Named viceroy of New Granada on February 20, 1810, he never took office: he was assigned to New Spain, where he entered the capital on September 14, 1810 and governed until March 4, 1813. Three days after his entry the Cry of Dolores broke out; he prohibited revolutionary publications, created police courts and military juntas in the provinces, and sent Calleja against the insurgents. He delayed the publication of the Constitution of Cádiz and decreed a state of siege. The Audiencia accused him of being soft on the rebellion, and the Junta of Cádiz of arbitrary measures. He was succeeded by Calleja and in Spain received the title of Marquis of La Reunión de Nueva España.

personas/vicente-filisola/resumen.texto: Military man born in the kingdom of Naples (around 1785 or 1789), who served Spain and joined the Plan of Iguala in 1821. As captain general and political chief of Guatemala from June 1822, he administered the annexation of Central America to the Mexican Empire, occupied San Salvador in February 1823 and convened the congress that declared independence. In 1836 he was second in command of the Mexican army in Texas. He was not president of the Federal Republic.

personas/juan-vicente-villacorta/resumen.texto: Merchant from Zacatecoluca and deputy to the constituent assembly of the United Provinces of Central America; he was part of the first and second triumvirates of the Executive Power (1823–1824) and head of state of El Salvador from December 13, 1824 to 1826. He introduced stamped paper (1825). He died in San Salvador in 1827 or in Guatemala in 1828, depending on the source.

personas/mariano-beltranena-y-llano/resu.texto: Guatemalan aristocrat, intendant of Nicaragua (1816–1819), federal vice president elected for 1825–1829, whom Arce called to exercise the Executive in 1828. Francisco Morazán entered Guatemala in April 1829 and overthrew him; he was exiled, lived for years in Cuba and died in Matanzas.

personas/jose-francisco-barrundia/resume.texto: Guatemalan liberal politician, editor of El Editor Constitucional, which Pedro Molina directed, and promoter of independence. With Morazán victorious, he was interim president of the Federal Republic from June 1829 until September 1830. He translated the Livingston code, which was promulgated in Guatemala in 1837, and died in New York as minister of Honduras.

personas/diego-vigil/resumen.texto: Lawyer from Tegucigalpa, head of state of Honduras (1828–1829) and of El Salvador (1836–1838), and last president of the Federal Republic of Central America: elected vice president in 1838 to succeed Gregorio Salazar, he took office when Morazán handed it over to him on February 1, 1839. With only El Salvador left in the federation, that state declared it dissolved on March 31, 1840, and his government ended. He died in Granada, Nicaragua.

personas/alonso-fernandez-de-bonilla/res.texto: Native of Córdoba, dean of the cathedral of Mexico, prosecutor and from 1583 inquisitor of the Holy Office of Mexico; he was sent as visitor general to Peru. There his presentation as archbishop of Mexico (1592) reached him, and there Toribio de Mogrovejo consecrated him in 1593. He never reached his see, which was governed in his name by the archdeacon Juan Cervantes, and he died in Lima in 1596 according to Bancroft or in 1600 according to Catholic-Hierarchy.

personas/garcia-de-santa-maria-mendoza/n.texto: García de Santa María Mendoza y Zúñiga

personas/garcia-de-santa-maria-mendoza/r.texto: Hieronymite of Alcalá de Henares, prior in Seville and elected general of his order in 1591. Appointed archbishop of Mexico in 1600 and consecrated in 1601, he died in the capital on October 5, 1606.

personas/jose-rafael-gallegos/resumen.texto: Landowner and merchant, born in Cartago or in Cesantes (Galicia), depending on the source. He presided over the Superior Governing Junta of Costa Rica (October 1822 to January 1823) and was vice head of state. Elected head of state by the Assembly in 1833 despite having only one vote, he governed until 1835 and again exercised the Executive between May 1845 and June 1846.

hechos/fundacion-de-santa-maria-la-antig.texto: Founding of Santa María la Antigua del Darién
Santa María la Antigua del Darién

The first stable Spanish city on the American mainland, founded in 1510 by Martín Fernández de Enciso and Vasco Núñez de Balboa in Darién (today Colombia), after defeating the cacique Cémaco and occupying his town. It was the seat of the first bishopric on the continent (1513) and the capital of Castilla del Oro until Pedrarias moved the government to Panama; it was abandoned in 1524.

hechos/balboa-llega-al-mar-del-sur/resum.texto: In September 1513 Vasco Núñez de Balboa crossed the Isthmus of Panama with about 190 Spaniards and hundreds of Indigenous guides and porters. On September 25 he saw from a ridge the ocean he called the South Sea, and days later he took possession of it in the Gulf of San Miguel. Along the way, according to Pedro Mártir de Anglería, he defeated the cacique Cuarecuá, who died with hundreds of his men, and had about forty Indigenous men accused of sodomy thrown to dogs.

hechos/castilla-del-oro-de-pedrarias/tit.texto: Governorship of Castilla del Oro of Pedrarias Dávila

hechos/castilla-del-oro-de-pedrarias/res.texto: The expedition of Pedrarias Dávila, of some 1,500 people, reached Darién in 1514 as the first large enterprise organized by the Crown on the mainland, with the Requerimiento as the legal instrument of the conquest. Hundreds of settlers soon died of hunger and disease, and the raids of his captains plundered and enslaved the chiefdoms of the isthmus, as denounced by Oviedo, who served as the colony’s veedor, and by Las Casas, whose death tolls are very high and cannot be verified.

hechos/fundacion-de-panama/resumen.texto: Pedrarias Dávila founded the city of Panama on August 15, 1519, next to a village of Indigenous fishermen on the Pacific coast, as the capital of Castilla del Oro. It became the base for expeditions to Nicaragua and Peru, the route for Peruvian silver to Nombre de Dios and Portobelo, and the seat of an audiencia from 1538. It was sacked and burned in 1671 during Henry Morgan’s attack, and rebuilt in 1673 on another site.

hechos/saqueo-de-portobelo-1668/titulo.texto: Sack of Portobelo by Henry Morgan

hechos/saqueo-de-portobelo-1668/resumen.texto: In July 1668 the privateer Henry Morgan, with about 500 men and a commission from the governor of Jamaica, took Portobelo by surprise, the port of the trade fairs with Peru. According to Exquemelin’s account, he used religious men and nuns as shields to storm a fort, and he tortured residents to reveal their goods; he collected a ransom of 100,000 pesos and withdrew.

hechos/saqueo-de-panama-1671/resumen.texto: At the end of 1670 Henry Morgan, with more than a thousand buccaneers, took the San Lorenzo castle at the mouth of the Chagres; in January 1671 he crossed the isthmus and defeated the Spanish militias in front of the city of Panama, which burned in a fire of disputed origin and was sacked for weeks. Because the action violated the 1670 peace treaty between Spain and England, Morgan was taken prisoner to London, though he was later knighted and named deputy governor of Jamaica.

hechos/colonia-escocesa-del-darien/resum.texto: The Company of Scotland, promoted by William Paterson, sent about 1,200 colonists in 1698 to found New Caledonia on the Caribbean coast of Darién, on lands Spain claimed and where the Guna lived, with whom they had good relations. Fevers, hunger and the lack of English support made it fail, and a second expedition capitulated to the Spanish in 1700; about 2,000 colonists died, and the bankruptcy weighed on the union of Scotland and England (1707).

hechos/pueblo-guna/resumen.texto: A Chibchan-speaking people of Darién and of the Caribbean coast of Panama and Colombia, organized in villages governed by congresses and chiefs (sailas). During the colonial period they resisted the Spaniards in Darién, traded, and sometimes allied with buccaneers, Scots and French; in the 19th century much of the population moved to the San Blas Islands.

hechos/revolucion-guna/resumen.texto: In February 1925 the Guna of the San Blas Islands, led by Nele Kantule and Simral Colman and with support from the American Richard Marsh, rose up against the Panamanian police who were repressing their customs. They killed police officers and Guna who supported the government, and proclaimed a Tule republic. An agreement reached with United States mediation ended the conflict and paved the way for the autonomous comarca recognized in 1938 and 1953.

hechos/nicaraos-y-chorotegas/resumen.texto: When the Spaniards arrived, the Pacific strip of Nicaragua and Nicoya was inhabited by Chorotegas (an Otomanguean-speaking people) and Nicaraos (a Nahuatl-speaking people), who had arrived from Mexico in the Postclassic period, in densely populated chiefdoms with markets, temples and cacao as money. Oviedo, who was there in 1527-1529, described their councils of elders, their trade, and also their wars, their slavery, their human sacrifices and the ritual consumption of captives’ flesh.

hechos/conquista-de-nicaragua/resumen.texto: In 1522-1523 Gil González Dávila traveled along the Pacific coast of Nicaragua, where he spoke with the cacique the chronicles call Nicarao and was attacked by the warriors of Diriangén. In 1524 Francisco Hernández de Córdoba, sent by Pedrarias, founded Granada and León; wars followed against Chorotegas, Nicaraos and other peoples, with Indigenous allies from Mexico, and disputes among conquistadors, until Pedrarias took over the government in 1527.

hechos/fundacion-de-granada-y-leon/resum.texto: Francisco Hernández de Córdoba founded Granada in 1524, beside Lake Cocibolca, and León, beside Lake Managua, in areas of dense Indigenous population. León was the capital of the province of Nicaragua until, after earthquakes and the activity of the Momotombo volcano, its residents abandoned it in 1610 and refounded it on its present site; its ruins, León Viejo, are a World Heritage Site.

hechos/trata-de-indios-de-nicaragua/titu.texto: Trade in Indigenous Slaves from Nicaragua

hechos/trata-de-indios-de-nicaragua/resu.texto: From 1526, governors and encomenderos of Nicaragua and Honduras branded as slaves Indigenous people taken in war or handed over by caciques as tribute, and shipped them to Panama and, from 1532, to Peru, where many died. The trade is documented in letters from bishops and royal officials, in Oviedo and Las Casas, and in the Crown’s prohibitions, which were enforced only with the New Laws and the presidency of Alonso López de Cerrato around 1550. Modern estimates of the number of people exported vary widely, from tens of thousands to nearly half a million, and Sherman, MacLeod and Newson consider it a central cause of the collapse of the population of the Nicaraguan Pacific.

hechos/pueblo-pipil/titulo.texto: The Pipil and the Lordship of Cuzcatlán

hechos/pueblo-pipil/resumen.texto: A Nahuatl-speaking people (Nahuat) of western and central El Salvador, who arrived from Mexico in Postclassic migrations and were organized in lordships such as Cuzcatlán and Izalco, with maize agriculture and large cacao production. After the conquest, Izalco’s cacao was the main wealth of the province in the 16th century; their language survives today with very few speakers.

hechos/conquista-de-cuzcatlan/resumen.texto: In June 1524 Pedro de Alvarado, with Nahua and Kaqchikel allies, entered Pipil territory and defeated them at Acajutla and Tacuzcalco, but did not manage to subdue them: they withdrew to the highlands and resisted. Gonzalo de Alvarado founded the villa of San Salvador in 1525, which was refounded in 1528 after new campaigns.

hechos/pueblo-lenca/resumen.texto: A people of the mountains of western and central Honduras and of eastern El Salvador, organized in lordships that allied with and fought against one another, with their own languages of disputed affiliation. They resisted the conquest in the 1537-1538 rebellion led by Lempira; afterward they were subjected to encomiendas and resettled into towns, and their languages were lost, although Lenca identity persists.

hechos/conquista-de-honduras/resumen.texto: Honduras was contested in 1524 by several expeditions: Gil González Dávila from the south and Cristóbal de Olid, sent by Cortés, who rebelled against him. Cortés himself arrived in 1525 after a march from Mexico during which he had Cuauhtémoc executed. Wars against the peoples of the interior, the slave trade and epidemics reduced the population; Francisco de Montejo and Alonso de Cáceres defeated Lempira’s rebellion, and Gracias a Dios (1536) and Comayagua (1537) were founded.

hechos/rebelion-de-lempira/resumen.texto: In 1537 the Lenca chief Lempira gathered peoples of western Honduras (according to Antonio de Herrera, some 30,000 warriors) and for months resisted, from the peñol of Cerquín, the forces of Francisco de Montejo and his Indigenous allies. Lempira died that year, treacherously during a negotiation according to Herrera or in combat according to a soldier’s probanza, and the uprising, which had spread to other areas of Honduras, was suppressed in 1538.

hechos/conquista-de-costa-rica/titulo.texto: Conquest of the Central Valley of Costa Rica

hechos/conquista-de-costa-rica/resumen.texto: After failed attempts from the 1520s onward, Juan de Cavallón entered the Central Valley of Costa Rica in 1561, and Juan Vázquez de Coronado completed the subjection of the Huetares and other chiefdoms between 1562 and 1564, largely through agreements with their leaders. Cartago was founded in 1563 as the capital of the province; the Talamanca region was never fully subjected.

hechos/rebelion-de-talamanca/resumen.texto: On September 29, 1709 the Bribri and Cabécar peoples of Talamanca, led by Pablo Presbere, rose against the Franciscan missionaries who were trying to resettle them: they killed two friars, soldiers and the wife of one of the friars, and burned fourteen churches. An expedition from Cartago captured Presbere and hundreds of Indigenous people, who were taken to the Central Valley; Presbere was executed by firing squad in Cartago in 1710, and Talamanca remained outside Spanish control.

hechos/reino-misquito/titulo.texto: The Miskito and the Kingdom of Mosquitia

hechos/reino-misquito/resumen.texto: The Miskito, a people of the Caribbean coast of Nicaragua and Honduras who incorporated Africans who arrived through shipwrecks and escapes (the “zambos misquitos”), allied from the 17th century with the English of Jamaica, who crowned their kings and supplied them with weapons. They attacked Spanish settlements and captured Indigenous people from other peoples to sell as slaves to the English. Great Britain kept a protectorate until 1860, and Nicaragua incorporated the region by force in 1894.

hechos/asentamiento-britanico-de-belice/.texto: From the mid-17th century British logwood and then mahogany cutters settled on the coast of Belize, on territory Spain claimed and where Maya peoples lived. The treaties of Paris (1763) and Versailles (1783) and the London convention (1786) recognized their right to cut timber without sovereignty; they depended on the labor of enslaved Africans, who were the majority of the population at the end of the 18th century. In 1798 they repelled a Spanish attack at St. George’s Caye, and in 1862 the settlement became the colony of British Honduras.

hechos/conquista-de-guatemala/resumen.texto: Pedro de Alvarado left Mexico at the end of 1523 with some 400 Spaniards and thousands of Nahua allies from Tlaxcala, Cholula, Mexico and other towns. In February 1524 he defeated the K’iche’ near Xelajú (Quetzaltenango), whose chief is remembered in the K’iche’ tradition as Tecún Umán (his historicity is disputed), and in March he burned the K’iche’ lords alive in Q’umarkaj. He allied with the Kaqchikels, enemies of the K’iche’ since they had separated from them around 1470, who rebelled in August 1524 over demands for gold and resisted until 1530, while the Mam, Tz’utujil, Poqomam and other peoples were subjected in campaigns in which Indigenous allies played a decisive role.

hechos/fundacion-de-santiago-de-guatemal.texto: Founding and Relocations of Santiago de Guatemala

Alvarado founded Santiago de los Caballeros de Guatemala on July 25, 1524, next to Iximché, the Kaqchikel capital; because of the rebellion of its former allies, the city moved in 1527 to the Almolonga valley (today Ciudad Vieja). It was destroyed in 1541 by a landslide from the Volcán de Agua, was refounded in 1543 in the Panchoy valley (today Antigua Guatemala), and after the earthquakes of 1773 the capital was moved in 1776 to the Valle de la Ermita, today Guatemala City.

hechos/destruccion-de-santiago-en-almolo.texto: Destruction of Santiago de Guatemala by the Volcán de Agua

On the night of September 10 to 11, 1541, after days of rain, an avalanche of water and mud came down from the Volcán de Agua and buried the city of Santiago, in Almolonga. The governor Beatriz de la Cueva, Alvarado’s widow, died, along with many Spanish and Indigenous residents; the account by the notary Juan Rodríguez, printed that year in Mexico by Juan Pablos, is considered the first news publication of the Americas.

hechos/verapaz/titulo.texto: Verapaz: The Project of Peaceful Conversion of Tezulutlán

hechos/verapaz/resumen.texto: In 1537 Bartolomé de las Casas and the Dominicans Pedro de Angulo and Luis de Cáncer agreed with the governor Alonso de Maldonado that the region of Tezulutlán, called the “land of war” for its resistance, would receive neither soldiers nor encomenderos if its towns peacefully accepted the friars. With the help of converted caciques, the region was incorporated without armed conquest and from 1547 was called Verapaz. The Dominican chronicler Remesal is the main source; other historians qualify the success because of the later forced concentration of towns and the wars against the Lacandones and Choles.

hechos/audiencia-de-guatemala/titulo.texto: Audiencia and Captaincy General of Guatemala

hechos/audiencia-de-guatemala/resumen.texto: A court and government created by the New Laws as the Audiencia de los Confines, installed in Gracias a Dios in 1544 and moved to Santiago de Guatemala in 1549. Its president, with the title of captain general, governed the Kingdom of Guatemala, from Chiapas to Costa Rica, under nominal dependence on the viceroy of New Spain. Under Alonso López de Cerrato (1548-1555) it freed thousands of enslaved Indigenous people and set new tribute rates.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-universidad-de-sa.texto: Founding of the University of San Carlos de Guatemala
University of San Carlos de Guatemala

Charles II founded the university by royal cédula of January 31, 1676, on the bequest that Bishop Francisco Marroquín had left for a college; it opened its courses in 1681 in Santiago de Guatemala, with chairs in theology, canon law, law, medicine and one Indigenous language. It was the first university in Central America and moved to Nueva Guatemala after the earthquakes of 1773.

hechos/rebelion-tzeltal-de-1712/resumen.texto: An uprising of about thirty Tzeltal, Tsotsil and Chol towns in the Altos de Chiapas, begun in Cancuc in August 1712 after the announcement of an apparition of the Virgin to the young María de la Candelaria. The rebels created their own Indigenous clergy, disavowed the Church and the king, and killed friars and Spanish residents; troops from Guatemala and Tabasco defeated them at the end of 1712, and the repression and famine that followed caused many deaths. Historians link it to the weight of tribute, the repartimientos of goods and ecclesiastical burdens.

hechos/terremotos-de-santa-marta/titulo.texto: Santa Marta Earthquakes and the Move of Guatemala's Capital

hechos/terremotos-de-santa-marta/resumen.texto: On July 29, 1773, Saint Martha's day, a series of earthquakes destroyed much of Santiago de Guatemala. After a long dispute between Captain General Martín de Mayorga, who favored the move, and Archbishop Pedro Cortés y Larraz, who opposed it, the Crown ordered the capital moved to the Ermita valley, where Nueva Guatemala de la Asunción was founded in 1776; the old city remained as Antigua Guatemala.

hechos/independencia-de-centroamerica/re.texto: On September 15, 1821, upon news of the Plan of Iguala and the independence of Chiapas, a junta of authorities and residents of Guatemala City declared independence from Spain, with Captain General Gabino Gaínza as political chief. In January 1822 most of the town councils approved annexation to the Mexican Empire, which San Salvador resisted and which Vicente Filísola's troops defeated; after Iturbide's fall, an assembly declared the absolute independence of the United Provinces of Central America on July 1, 1823. Panama became independent from Spain on November 28, 1821, and joined Gran Colombia.

hechos/republica-federal-de-centroameric.texto: Federation of Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica organized by the Constitution of 1824; in April of that year its assembly abolished slavery, one of the first abolitions in the Americas. Wars between liberals and conservatives, with Francisco Morazán and Rafael Carrera as leaders, dissolved it between 1838 and 1841.

hechos/llegada-de-los-doce-franciscanos/.texto: Arrival of the Twelve Franciscans in Mexico

In 1524 twelve Franciscans led by Martín de Valencia arrived, among them Motolinía; according to the chronicles, Cortés received them on his knees before Indigenous lords. They began systematic evangelization: schools for sons of nobles, language learning, mass baptisms and the destruction of temples and images; the Dominicans (1526) and the Augustinians (1533) followed.

hechos/primera-audiencia-de-mexico/resum.texto: Tribunal and government presided over by Nuño de Guzmán, with the judges (oidores) Juan Ortiz de Matienzo and Diego Delgadillo, which governed New Spain between 1528 and 1530. Zumárraga and others denounced its abuses: branding and selling Indians as slaves, many of them sent to the Antilles from Pánuco, excessive tribute, and persecution of Cortés's supporters. The Crown replaced it with a second Audiencia (1531–1535), presided over by Sebastián Ramírez de Fuenleal, with Vasco de Quiroga as oidor.

hechos/escuela-de-san-jose-de-los-natura.texto: School of San José de los Naturales

Franciscan school founded by Pedro de Gante around 1527 next to the convent of San Francisco in Mexico City, where Indigenous children were taught reading, writing, singing, music and trades such as painting, carpentry and tailoring. Its open-air chapel gathered thousands of Indigenous worshippers, and its workshops trained the craftsmen of the religious works.

hechos/esclavitud-indigena-en-nueva-espa.texto: Enslavement of Indigenous People in New Spain

After the conquest, Spaniards branded as slaves Indigenous people taken in war and others bought as slaves “de rescate,” a form that already existed in Mesoamerica under other rules (the Nahua tlacotin). The Crown prohibited it in 1530, allowed it again in 1534 and abolished it with the New Laws (1542); around 1550 the Audiencia freed most Indigenous slaves, although the enslavement of captives continued in the northern frontier wars. Nuño de Guzmán sent thousands of slaves from Pánuco to the Antilles (1527–1529).

hechos/encomienda-y-repartimiento-en-nue.texto: Encomienda and Repartimiento of Labor in New Spain

From 1522 Cortés assigned towns in encomiendas, which gave Spaniards the tribute and labor of Indigenous people in exchange for protection and doctrine. The New Laws (1542) forbade granting new encomiendas and inheriting them, but in the face of resistance from encomenderos the Crown revoked the ban on inheritance in 1545; a cédula of 1549 prohibited personal service, and over time many encomiendas passed to the Crown. From the 1550s forced labor was organized by repartimiento: towns had to send, in rotation, a share of their men to public works, farming and mines in exchange for a wage set by the authorities. The agricultural repartimiento was abolished in 1633 and the mining one continued; the abuses are documented in complaints by the towns themselves, such as the Kingsborough Codex.

hechos/pueblos-hospital-de-santa-fe/resu.texto: Vasco de Quiroga founded with his own salary the pueblo-hospital of Santa Fe, next to Mexico City (1532), and that of Santa Fe de la Laguna, on the shore of Lake Pátzcuaro (1533), and promoted hospitals in many Purépecha towns. They gathered Indigenous families with common property, shift work, teaching of trades and a hospital for the sick and travelers. Quiroga defended them for decades in lawsuits with encomenderos and with the Audiencia.

hechos/fundacion-del-hospital-de-jesus/t.texto: Founding of the Hospital de Jesús

hechos/fundacion-del-hospital-de-jesus/r.texto: Hospital founded by Hernán Cortés around 1524 in Mexico City, next to the place where, according to tradition, he met Moctezuma in 1519. It treated poor patients, Cortés left it income in his will, and it still operates today, which is why it is considered the oldest hospital in the Americas in continuous use.

hechos/fundacion-de-puebla/titulo.texto: Founding of Puebla de los Ángeles

hechos/fundacion-de-puebla/resumen.texto: City founded in April 1531 by the second Audiencia and the Franciscans, with Motolinía present, as a town of Spaniards without encomiendas who would live from their own work, in a valley between Tlaxcala and Cholula; Indigenous workers from neighboring towns built it. It was the second city of New Spain, seat of a bishopric, of obrajes (textile workshops) and of talavera ware.

hechos/fundacion-del-colegio-de-tlatelol.texto: Founding of the College of Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco
College of Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco

Franciscan college opened on January 6, 1536, with support from Zumárraga and Viceroy Mendoza, for sons of the Indigenous nobility, who studied Latin, rhetoric, philosophy, music and medicine. Antonio Valeriano and the Nahua collaborators of Sahagún were trained there, and the Codex de la Cruz-Badiano was made, although some Spaniards opposed teaching Latin to Indians. From the 1570s, with epidemics, a lack of funds and the refusal to ordain Indigenous priests, it declined until it became a school for basic literacy.

hechos/proceso-de-don-carlos-ometochtzin.texto: Trial and Execution of Don Carlos Ometochtzin

Trial that Zumárraga, as apostolic inquisitor, conducted in 1539 against the lord of Texcoco, Don Carlos Ometochtzin, accused of keeping idols, living with a concubine and urging nobles to return to the old religion. He was burned in the main square of Mexico City on November 30, 1539. The punishment was criticized from Spain, and the case contributed to the Inquisition established in 1571 having no jurisdiction over Indians.

hechos/primera-imprenta-de-america/titul.texto: First Printing Press in the Americas

hechos/primera-imprenta-de-america/resum.texto: In 1539 the printer Juan Pablos, sent by the Sevillian Juan Cromberger at the request of Zumárraga and Viceroy Mendoza, set up the first documented printing press on the continent in the Casa de las Campanas in Mexico City. Until 1560 it printed at least 35 books, mainly doctrinal works, confessionals, grammars and vocabularies in Castilian, Nahuatl and other Indigenous languages; Lima had its first press only in 1584.

hechos/fundacion-del-colegio-de-san-nico.texto: Founding of the College of San Nicolás Obispo

College founded by Vasco de Quiroga in Pátzcuaro around 1540 to train priests who knew the Purépecha language; it moved to Valladolid (today Morelia) in 1580. Miguel Hidalgo was its student, professor and rector. It is the forerunner of the Universidad Michoacana de San Nicolás de Hidalgo.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-universidad-de-me.texto: Founding of the Royal University of Mexico
Royal and Pontifical University of Mexico

A royal cédula signed in the name of Charles V on September 21, 1551 created the University of Mexico with the privileges of Salamanca; it opened its courses in 1553 with Viceroy Luis de Velasco and in 1595 received the title of pontifical. It taught theology, canon law, law, medicine and the arts, and had a chair in Nahuatl. Noble Indigenous people could study there, but its students were mostly Creoles. It closed permanently in 1865.

hechos/hospital-real-de-naturales/titulo.texto: Founding of the Hospital Real de Naturales

hechos/hospital-real-de-naturales/resume.texto: Hospital for Indigenous people founded in Mexico City by a cédula of 1553 and opened with Viceroy Luis de Velasco, later financed by a contribution of half a real from Indigenous tributaries and by the income of a theater. It treated thousands of patients during the epidemics, and in 1576 Francisco Hernández and other physicians performed autopsies there on victims of the cocoliztli.

hechos/concilios-provinciales-mexicanos/.texto: Assemblies of the bishops of New Spain convened in 1555 and 1565 by Archbishop Montúfar and in 1585 by Pedro Moya de Contreras. The first forbade ordaining Indians, mestizos and mulattos as priests; the third, in force until the 19th century, regulated doctrine, sacraments and the use of Indigenous languages, condemned abuses against Indians and, when consulted by the viceroy, questioned the justice of the war of fire and blood against the Chichimecas.

hechos/congregaciones-de-indios/resumen.texto: Relocation of dispersed Indigenous populations into new towns laid out on a grid, with a church and a cabildo, in order to evangelize, collect tribute and organize labor. There were two major campaigns: around 1550–1564, driven by the friars and Viceroy Velasco, and between 1598 and 1607, after the epidemics, with congregation judges. Many families resisted or returned to their former settlements, and the lands left vacant often passed into Spanish hands.

hechos/republica-de-indios/resumen.texto: Legal order that separated Indigenous towns, the “república de indios,” from the “república de españoles”: the towns had their own cabildo with Indigenous governor, alcaldes and regidores, communal lands, community treasuries and special legal protection, and in exchange they paid tribute and provided labor. In theory Spaniards, Blacks and mestizos could not live in them; the cabildos left thousands of documents in Nahuatl, Mixtec, Maya and other languages. The separation was never fully achieved; mestizaje and haciendas eroded it, and the Constitution of Cádiz (1812) formally abolished it.

hechos/juzgado-general-de-indios/resumen.texto: Special court of New Spain for Indigenous lawsuits, with a brief, oral and free procedure for litigants, financed by the “medio real de ministros” paid by each tributary. It was organized between 1585 and 1607, mainly under Viceroy Luis de Velasco the younger, drawing on the custom of viceroys since Mendoza of hearing Indians' complaints in person, and it operated until 1820. Borah and Owensby show that Indigenous people used it on a massive scale, including against their own caciques and against other communities.

hechos/inquisicion-de-mexico/titulo.texto: Tribunal of the Inquisition in Mexico

hechos/inquisicion-de-mexico/resumen.texto: Tribunal of the Holy Office established in Mexico in 1571, with Pedro Moya de Contreras as its first inquisitor. By royal order Indians were placed outside its jurisdiction, and their religious offenses passed to the bishops. It pursued mainly bigamy, blasphemy, witchcraft, Judaizers and Protestants: at the auto de fe of 1574 it punished English sailors from Hawkins's fleet, and in 1596 and 1649 it burned Jewish converts such as Luis de Carvajal the Younger. One estimate speaks of around 50 executions over its whole history; it was abolished in 1820.

hechos/epidemias-de-cocoliztli/resumen.texto: Two major epidemics of a fever with hemorrhages, which the Nahuas called cocoliztli (“pestilence”), killed a large part of the Indigenous population of New Spain in 1545–1548 and 1576–1580, while Spaniards fell ill much less. Chroniclers give figures from hundreds of thousands to millions of deaths, and Acuña-Soto and colleagues (2002) estimate between 5 and 15 million in 1545, a figure that depends on how large the population is assumed to have been beforehand. The cause is debated: Acuña-Soto proposes a local hemorrhagic fever worsened by a severe drought, and ancient DNA from Teposcolula (Vågene and colleagues, 2018) identified Salmonella Paratyphi C, the cause of an enteric fever that may have come from Europe (it was found in Norway around the year 1200).

hechos/caida-de-la-poblacion-del-centro-.texto: Decline of the Indigenous Population of Central Mexico

The Indigenous population of central Mexico fell during the 16th century due to epidemics (smallpox in 1520, measles in 1531, cocoliztli in 1545 and 1576), wars, forced labor, famine and social disorganization, bottoming out around 1620. The figures are disputed: Cook and Borah calculated about 25 million for 1518 and a little over one million for 1605; Rosenblat proposed about 4.5 million for all of Mexico in 1492, and Zambardino (1980) between 5 and 10 million for the center in 1519. Most authors accept a drop of between two-thirds and nine-tenths, with epidemics as the main cause.

hechos/epidemia-de-matlazahuatl/resumen.texto: Epidemic of a fever that the Nahuas called matlazáhuatl, later identified with typhus or other fevers with no consensus, which killed tens of thousands of people in 1736–1739 in Mexico City and the center of the viceroyalty, mainly Indigenous people. In 1737 the city swore the Virgin of Guadalupe in as its patroness to stop it, a key step in the expansion of her cult.

hechos/esclavitud-africana-en-nueva-espa.texto: From the conquest on, enslaved Africans arrived in New Spain, mainly through Veracruz and in greater numbers between 1595 and 1640, under Portuguese asientos; Curtin (1969) estimated some 200,000 for the whole colony. They worked on sugar mills, obrajes, mines, estates and urban houses, and many fled or won their freedom. The palenque of Yanga, near Córdoba, resisted a Spanish expedition in 1609 and later obtained recognition as a free town, San Lorenzo de los Negros (between 1618 and 1641, depending on the sources). In 1612 the Audiencia had more than thirty Africans and mulattos accused of conspiring to rise up hanged in Mexico City. Around 1803 Humboldt counted only about 6,000 slaves, when most Afro-descendants were already free and mixed with other groups. Hidalgo decreed abolition in 1810, and a decree by Vicente Guerrero made it general in Mexico in 1829.

hechos/descubrimiento-de-la-plata-de-zac.texto: In September 1546 an expedition led by Juan de Tolosa, with Indigenous guides, found the silver veins of Zacatecas, which within a few years attracted Spanish miners, paid and forced Indigenous laborers and enslaved Africans. The boom opened the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro to the north and set off the Chichimeca War; Zacatecas was for decades the main mining center of New Spain.

hechos/guerra-chichimeca/resumen.texto: Half-century war between the Spaniards, with Otomí, Purépecha and Nahua allies, and the nomadic and semi-nomadic peoples collectively called Chichimecas (Guachichiles, Zacatecos, Guamares, Pames and others), triggered by the opening of the silver road to Zacatecas. The Chichimecas attacked convoys and estates, and the Spaniards responded with presidios, campaigns and the enslavement of captives, whose legitimacy theologians and the Third Mexican Council debated. It ended with the “peace by purchase” of Viceroys Villamanrique and Velasco the younger (1585–1600), which handed out food, clothing and land and settled Tlaxcalan colonists among the Chichimecas.

hechos/metodo-de-patio/resumen.texto: In 1554, in Pachuca, Bartolomé de Medina put into practice on a large scale the amalgamation of silver with mercury, salt and other reagents in open-air patios. The method made it possible to use poor ores and multiplied silver production in Mexico and, from the 1570s, in Peru. It depended on mercury from Almadén and Huancavelica and poisoned many workers.

hechos/galeon-de-manila/resumen.texto: Shipping line between Manila and Acapulco, opened in 1565 when Andrés de Urdaneta found the return route across the North Pacific. It carried American silver to Asia and brought back Chinese silks, porcelain and spices, as well as free and enslaved people from Asia. It linked America, Asia and Europe regularly for the first time. It operated until 1815.

hechos/tornaviaje-de-urdaneta/resumen.texto: Andrés de Urdaneta, pilot of Legazpi's expedition to the Philippines, left Cebu on June 1, 1565 and, sailing north to latitudes off Japan to take advantage of the westerly winds, reached Acapulco on October 8. It was the first planned return from Asia to America across the Pacific. Alonso de Arellano, who had separated from the fleet, had arrived earlier, in August, by a similar route.

hechos/rebelion-de-los-tepehuanes/resume.texto: Uprising of the Tepehuanes of Nueva Vizcaya (Durango), led by religious leaders who announced the expulsion of the Spaniards. It began in November 1616 with the killing of several Jesuit and Franciscan missionaries, settlers and Christian Indigenous people. The repression, with Indigenous allies, lasted until 1620, with many deaths on both sides and the enslavement of prisoners.

hechos/misiones-jesuitas-del-noroeste/ti.texto: Jesuit Missions of Northwestern New Spain

hechos/misiones-jesuitas-del-noroeste/re.texto: The Jesuits worked as missionaries from 1591 in Sinaloa and Sonora, from 1687 in Pimería Alta with Eusebio Kino, and from 1697 in Baja California with Juan María de Salvatierra (Loreto mission). The missions gathered semi-nomadic peoples into towns with a church, crops and livestock, under the authority of the fathers and presidio soldiers. There were rebellions (Pima in 1695 and 1751, Pericú in 1734), and epidemics greatly reduced the population of Baja California. After the expulsion of 1767 the missions passed to Franciscans and Dominicans.

hechos/culto-de-guadalupe/titulo.texto: The Cult of Guadalupe and the Debate over the Apparitions

hechos/culto-de-guadalupe/resumen.texto: According to tradition, the Virgin appeared in December 1531 to the Indigenous man Juan Diego on the Tepeyac hill and left her image on his tilma. Documents show a chapel with a venerated image from at least 1556, but the account of the apparitions was first printed in 1648 (Sánchez) and 1649 (Lasso de la Vega). García Icazbalceta (1883) and Poole (1995) maintain that it took shape in the 17th century, and defenders of its historicity invoke oral tradition, the Codex Escalada and the attribution of the Nican mopohua to Valeriano. Devotion grew with the epidemic of 1737, and in 1754 Pope Benedict XIV approved her patronage over New Spain.

hechos/desague-de-huehuetoca/titulo.texto: Huehuetoca Drainage and the Flood of 1629

hechos/desague-de-huehuetoca/resumen.texto: To protect Mexico City from the floods of its lakes, in 1607 Viceroy Luis de Velasco the younger commissioned Enrico Martínez to build a tunnel and canal through Huehuetoca toward the Tula River. Thousands of Indigenous workers under repartimiento dug it in a few months. The tunnel became blocked, and in September 1629 a flood began that kept the city under water until 1634, with many deaths and the emigration of part of the population. The work became an open cut, finished at the end of the 18th century.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-biblioteca-palafo.texto: On September 5, 1646, Bishop Juan de Palafox donated his nearly 5,000 books to the colleges of Puebla, on the condition that they be open to anyone who wanted to read them. It is considered the first public library in the Americas, and it preserves its 18th-century baroque hall with about 45,000 volumes.

hechos/motin-de-1692/resumen.texto: On June 8, 1692, amid a shortage of maize caused by rains and plagues, a crowd of Indians, mestizos, mulattos and poor Spaniards attacked and set fire to the viceregal palace and the cabildo houses. Carlos de Sigüenza y Góngora saved part of the archive and wrote an account very hostile to the Indians. The repression included executions, a temporary ban on pulque, and an order that Indigenous people return to live in their barrios, outside the Spanish city grid.

hechos/sociedad-de-castas/titulo.texto: The Caste Society and Casta Paintings

hechos/sociedad-de-castas/resumen.texto: In New Spain people were classified by their Spanish, Indigenous and African ancestry (mestizos, castizos, mulattos, moriscos and other “castas”), with effects on tribute, access to offices, guilds and religious orders, and marriage. In the 18th century dozens of series of “casta paintings” were produced, such as Miguel Cabrera's (1763), mainly for a European public. Historians agree that the categories were more flexible in practice than in the paintings: the records show changes of quality according to place, wealth and reputation.

hechos/rebelion-de-canek/resumen.texto: In November 1761, during a festival in Cisteil (Yucatán), the Maya Jacinto Uc de los Santos proclaimed himself king under the name Canek and called for the expulsion of the Spaniards. Militias took the town days later, with hundreds of Maya dead. Canek was executed in Mérida on December 14, other leaders were hanged, and dozens of prisoners were whipped and mutilated by having an ear cut off.

hechos/visita-de-galvez/titulo.texto: General Inspection of José de Gálvez

hechos/visita-de-galvez/resumen.texto: General inspection of New Spain commissioned by Charles III to José de Gálvez, who reorganized the treasury (tobacco monopoly, customs, alcabalas), carried out the expulsion of the Jesuits and the repression of 1767, and organized the occupation of Alta California (1769). As minister of the Indies (1776–1787) he extended his reforms: intendancies, the Comandancia de las Provincias Internas and free trade, which increased revenue and displaced Creoles from offices.

hechos/expulsion-de-los-jesuitas-de-nuev.texto: Expulsion of the Jesuits from New Spain and the Riots of 1767

On June 25, 1767, Charles III's order to expel the Jesuits was carried out in New Spain: hundreds of religious left for exile, among them Clavijero and Landívar, and their colleges, haciendas and missions passed to other orders or to the Crown. There were riots in San Luis Potosí, Guanajuato, Pátzcuaro and other cities, which the visitor José de Gálvez repressed. According to his own report, 85 people were hanged and hundreds sentenced to whipping, prison or exile.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-academia-de-san-c.texto: Founding of the Academy of San Carlos

First academy of fine arts in the Americas, born in 1781 from the engraving school of the Mint of Mexico, approved by Charles III in 1783 and inaugurated in 1785. It taught painting, sculpture, architecture and engraving according to neoclassicism, with professors such as Manuel Tolsá.

hechos/real-expedicion-botanica-a-nueva-.texto: Royal Botanical Expedition to New Spain

Scientific expedition of the Crown led by Martín Sessé, with José Mariano Mociño and the Mexican illustrators Atanasio Echeverría and Juan de Dios Vicente de la Cerda, which traveled through New Spain, the Antilles, Central America and the Pacific coast as far as Nootka. It created the Botanical Garden and the chair of botany in Mexico, and gathered thousands of descriptions and illustrations of plants, which remained unpublished until the late 19th century.

hechos/censo-de-revillagigedo/resumen.texto: First general census of New Spain, ordered by the viceroy, the Count of Revillagigedo, which counted the population by intendancy with data on caste (Spanish, Indian, mestizo, mulatto), occupation and age, although some provinces remained incomplete. Humboldt used it to estimate in 1803 some 5.8 million inhabitants, of whom about 2.5 million were Indigenous.

hechos/fundacion-del-real-seminario-de-m.texto: Founding of the Royal Seminary of Mining

Technical school created by the Royal Mining Tribunal and opened on January 1, 1792 under the direction of Fausto de Elhuyar, with chairs in mathematics, physics, chemistry and mineralogy. Andrés Manuel del Río taught there, and Humboldt praised it in 1803. Its seat, the Palacio de Minería designed by Manuel Tolsá, was built between 1797 and 1813.

hechos/descubrimiento-del-vanadio/resume.texto: In 1801 Andrés Manuel del Río, a professor at the Seminario de Minería, found a new element in a lead ore from Zimapán, which he called erythronium. An analysis by the French chemist Collet-Descotils mistakenly attributed it to chromium, and Del Río withdrew his finding. Nils Sefström rediscovered it in 1830 as vanadium, and Del Río's priority was later recognized.

hechos/real-expedicion-filantropica-de-l.texto: Royal Philanthropic Expedition of the Vaccine

Expedition financed by the Crown and led by Francisco Javier de Balmis, which left A Coruña on November 30, 1803 with 22 foundlings and the matron Isabel Zendal, to carry the smallpox vaccine alive by passing it arm to arm. It vaccinated in Puerto Rico, Venezuela, Cuba and New Spain, where vaccine boards were created. In 1805 it went on to the Philippines with 26 Mexican children, reaching Macao and Canton; its South American branch, under José Salvany, reached as far as Peru and Charcas. It is estimated to have vaccinated hundreds of thousands of people.

hechos/consolidacion-de-vales-reales/res.texto: Royal cédula of 1804 that required the ecclesiastical institutions of New Spain to hand over to the Crown the capital they had lent to landowners, merchants and miners, to pay Spain's war debt. Debtors had to repay the loans all at once or lose their property. The measure hit mainly middling Creole property owners, was denounced by the bishop-elect Manuel Abad y Queipo, and fed discontent before 1808. It was suspended in 1808.

hechos/crisis-de-1808-en-mexico/resumen.texto: When the Bayonne abdications became known, the Creole city council of Mexico City, with Francisco Primo de Verdad and Fray Melchor de Talamantes, proposed a junta to govern in the king's name, and Viceroy José de Iturrigaray seemed to accept it. On September 15, 1808, Peninsular merchants led by Gabriel de Yermo deposed him by force, and Primo de Verdad and Talamantes died in prison. The coup closed the legal path and opened the way to the conspiracies of Valladolid (1809) and Querétaro (1810).

hechos/toma-de-la-alhondiga-de-granadita.texto: Capture of the Alhóndiga de Granaditas

On September 28, 1810, Hidalgo's insurgent crowd, made up mainly of Indigenous people and mine and hacienda workers, took the granary of Guanajuato, where the intendant Juan Antonio Riaño had taken refuge with soldiers and Spanish and Creole families. Riaño, the defenders and numerous civilians died, and the city was sacked; Allende reproached Hidalgo for these excesses. When Calleja retook the city in November he ordered reprisal executions, and from 1811 the heads of Hidalgo, Allende, Aldama and Jiménez hung from the corners of the Alhóndiga until 1821.

hechos/batalla-de-puente-de-calderon/res.texto: On January 17, 1811, near Guadalajara, the royalist army of Félix Calleja, of about 6,000 men, defeated the forces of Hidalgo and Allende, tens of thousands of people, mostly poorly armed. The insurgent leaders fled north and were captured at Acatita de Baján in March.

hechos/ejecucion-de-hidalgo/titulo.texto: Trial and Execution of Miguel Hidalgo

hechos/ejecucion-de-hidalgo/resumen.texto: Captured in March 1811, Hidalgo was tried in Chihuahua by a military court and stripped of his orders by the ecclesiastical authority. In his statements he acknowledged having ordered the deaths of hundreds of Spanish prisoners in Valladolid and Guadalajara. He was shot on July 30, 1811, after Allende, Aldama and Jiménez.

hechos/congreso-de-chilpancingo/resumen.texto: Insurgent congress convened by Morelos in Chilpancingo on September 13, 1813, which named him generalísimo and declared independence on November 6. Pursued by the royalists, it sanctioned the Constitution of 1814 in Apatzingán. It was the first attempt to give the insurgency a representative government.

hechos/ejecucion-de-morelos/resumen.texto: Captured at Temalaca in November 1815 while protecting the congress's retreat, Morelos was tried by the ecclesiastical jurisdiction and the Inquisition, which declared him a heretic and degraded him, and by a military court. He was shot in San Cristóbal Ecatepec on December 22, 1815.

hechos/independencia-de-mexico/resumen.texto: War begun with Hidalgo's uprising in September 1810 and continued by Morelos, Guerrero and other insurgent leaders against the royalist army, with violence on both sides. After years of guerrilla warfare, the royalist officer Agustín de Iturbide allied with Guerrero in the Plan of Iguala (1821), won over almost the entire army and entered Mexico City with the Army of the Three Guarantees on September 27, 1821. The next day the act of independence of the Mexican Empire was signed. Spain recognized it in 1836.

hechos/primer-imperio-mexicano/resumen.texto: Constitutional monarchy born from independence, with Iturbide as regent and, from May 1822, as Emperor Agustín I. In January 1822 the former kingdom of Guatemala was annexed to it. At odds with the congress, which he dissolved, and with the Plan of Casa Mata, Iturbide abdicated in March 1823. Mexico was organized as a federal republic (1824), and Central America, except Chiapas, separated.
